title: Learned satellite mapping characterizes mixed floating-debris accumulation along the Tisza
summary: A support-vector classifier applied to 61 Sentinel-2 images mapped mixed natural and human-made floating-debris patches along 175 kilometers of the Middle Tisza River. The estimates identified a large persistent accumulation upstream of Kisköre Dam and changes across years and river stages. Moderate test performance, coarse pixels and biased visibility of large patches limit these estimates; they are not a plastic-mass inventory or proof that the dam caused the pattern.
ai_technology: RBF support-vector classification of multispectral satellite pixels

evidence.tested: Training/validation used 1,974 labeled satellite pixels with an 80:20 random split; three separate litter-patch regions were used for size/generalization testing against higher-resolution imagery. The selected SVC had F1 approximately 0.62 on that broader test, below its random-pixel validation result. The model was then applied to 61 images from 2015–2021 across a 175-kilometer reach to estimate patch distributions and temporal changes.
evidence.unknown: Mixed debris includes substantial natural vegetation and wood; artificial litter cannot be separately quantified. Labels emphasized large persistent accumulations, and reference imagery differed in acquisition time. Spatially correlated pixels, tuning on limited data, false positives from vegetation/shadows/structures and missed sub-pixel patches constrain estimates. Three patch regions do not establish broad independent geographic validation. Temporal map patterns are model-derived observations, without independent field verification of every mapped patch or causal attribution to dam operation.
evidence.ai_role: The learned SVC separated debris-like from non-debris pixel signatures across repeated satellite observations, enabling the represented regional spatial and temporal accumulation analysis beyond the detector leaderboard.
